summary: Proposes a differentiated services per-domain behavior whose traffic may be starved, and is forwarded with lower priority than ordinary best-effort traffic. This lets an operator strictly limit the impact of that traffic on everything else. It is informational and has been replaced by RFC 8622.

eli5.summary: Some Internet traffic is like trash being taken out when nobody else needs the road. This describes a way to mark such low-urgency traffic so it never slows regular traffic. RFC 8622 has replaced it.

questions: how does le pdb protect best effort traffic
when should i mark traffic as lower effort
what happens to lower effort packets when the network is congested
subtitle: A way to mark non-critical traffic so it never blocks important traffic.

tldr.problem: Networks carry both critical and non-critical traffic. Bulk data like peer-to-peer downloads can consume all available bandwidth and starve important applications like video calls, even when marked with normal best-effort treatment.
tldr.mechanism: Lower Effort (LE) is a differentiated services per-domain behavior that treats marked traffic as lower priority than best-effort. LE traffic only gets bandwidth when no higher-priority traffic needs it, or gets only a small configured share.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can protect critical applications by marking bulk traffic as LE, ensuring it gets dropped or delayed in favor of regular traffic. RFC 8622 later replaced this with refined guidance.

facts.label: Traffic handling
facts.value: Starved or rate-limited when other traffic present

today: RFC 3662 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 8622 in June 2020. However, the LE concept remains widely used in network QoS configuration, and the implementation techniques described here are standard practice.

sections.title: What is Lower Effort?
sections.content:
Differentiated Services (DiffServ) lets routers mark packets with different priority levels. Most traffic gets best-effort treatment: the network makes a good-faith effort to deliver it, but gives it equal footing with all other best-effort traffic.

The Lower Effort (LE) per-domain behavior (PDB) is a lower tier. LE traffic is delivered only when no other traffic is waiting, or only consumes a small configured fraction of the link. Network operators can use LE to protect regular traffic from being starved by bulk traffic like file sharing or web crawlers.

The trade-off is clear: LE traffic may not arrive at all if the network is congested. Applications using LE must tolerate delays or loss.
sections.eli5: Lower Effort means 'deliver this when you have time, but ignore it completely if more important stuff is waiting.'

sections.title: How Lower Effort Works
sections.content:
A router implements LE using a queuing discipline. The simplest approach is a priority queue: LE packets sit in a separate queue that only sends traffic when the higher-priority (best-effort) queue is empty. This can starve LE completely.

An alternative is weighted scheduling. Best-effort traffic gets 90% of the link, and LE traffic gets 10%. This guarantees some throughput but never lets LE traffic exceed its share. A router can also use weighted random early drop (WRED) or other active queue management to drop more LE packets as congestion increases.

The RFC does not mandate a specific implementation. What matters is that LE traffic never interferes with other traffic when the link is busy.
sections.eli5: The router decides: either serve LE packets only when nothing else is waiting, or give them a tiny slice of bandwidth they can never exceed.

sections.title: Marking and Configuration
sections.content:
Packets destined for LE treatment are marked with a DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point). The RFC suggests using Class Selector 1 (DSCP = 001000) if a standard marking is needed, but operators can choose other DSCPs as long as their routers are configured consistently.

Unlike some DiffServ behaviors, LE does not require traffic shaping or policing at the network edge. If a packet arrives marked as LE, the routers accept it. Only if the network is congested does LE traffic get preferentially dropped. This simplicity is a strength: operators do not need to police LE traffic the way they police higher-priority traffic.
sections.eli5: A packet is marked with a label that says 'I am low priority.' Routers read the label and treat the packet as expendable.

sections.title: Uses and Examples
sections.content:
The RFC describes several use cases. Multimedia applications: A network manager wants to allow video or audio streaming but without letting it starve TCP applications. The excess video traffic goes to LE. Bulk transfer: Netnews, peer-to-peer file sharing, and web crawler traffic can be marked LE so universities and enterprises can run these services without degrading user experience. Content distribution: Bulk transfers of frequently updated content (like software updates) can use LE.

LE is not a way to drop unwanted traffic. It is a tool to allow low-value traffic to coexist with critical traffic. LE traffic should only be used for applications that genuinely can tolerate disruption.
sections.eli5: If you want to download a big file but do not care when it finishes, mark it as LE. If you want to download a file and it matters that you finish quickly, use regular traffic.

sections.title: Status and Later Developments
sections.content:
RFC 3662 is Informational, not a standard. It describes a technique operators can use without requiring equipment changes, since most DiffServ-capable routers already support the PHBs (Per-Hop Behaviors) it mentions. The RFC includes simulation results showing that LE protects best-effort traffic effectively across different implementations.

The document notes that LE was previously called bulk handling, but was renamed to be more generic. The authors received suggestions for creating a new PHB but chose to show that existing PHBs could deliver the desired behavior without standardization overhead.
sections.eli5: This is a how-to guide, not a hard rule. Network managers can start using these ideas today with routers they already have.
